Q: in the MASS::boxcox function, I often get the dreaded "'data' must be a data.frame, environment, or list" error erroneously A:

tl;dr you have to name your data frame something other than df, so that it doesn't collide with a built-in R object.

The error itself arises from line 526 of src/library/stats/R/models.R.

This is arguably a bug, or at least an "infelicity" (sensu Bill Venables), in MASS::boxcox, but it is also an illustration of why it's good to avoid name overlaps between your variables and built-in objects. (I've submitted a bug report.)

Continuing with your example:

dff <- df  ## rename your data frame
lmod <- lm(y~x, data=dff)
boxcox(lmod)

Error in boxcox.default(lmod) : response variable must be positive

This error happens because you constructed a slightly inappropriate example (which was fine for showing what you wanted).

lmod <- lm(abs(y)~x, data=dff)
boxcox(lmod)  ## works

We can get a hint of what's going on by looking at the output of traceback():

12: stop("'data' must be a data.frame, environment, or list")
11: model.frame.default(formula = y ~ x, data = df, drop.unused.levels = TRUE)
10: stats::model.frame(formula = y ~ x, data = df, drop.unused.levels = TRUE)
9: eval(mf, parent.frame())
8: eval(mf, parent.frame())
7: lm(formula = y ~ x, data = df, y = TRUE, qr = TRUE)
6: eval(call, parent.frame())
5: eval(call, parent.frame())
4: update.default(object, y = TRUE, qr = TRUE, ...)
3: update(object, y = TRUE, qr = TRUE, ...)
2: boxcox.lm(lmod)
1: boxcox(lmod)
  • boxcox is calling update() to make sure the fitted model has all the components it needs (especially the stored QR decomposition)
  • update() is re-calling lm()
  • lm() is calling model.frame()
  • by the time we get there, model.frame() is being evaluated in an environment where it sees the built-in df (in the stats package) before it sees your data frame (in .GlobalEnv).

It would take just a little more work than I feel like doing right now to establish exactly what all those parent.frame() invocations are seeing. From within the lm() call (you can get there by setting options(error = recover), you can see that the enclosing environment of the parent frame parent.frame()$enclos is <environment:base>. I'm not quite sure how we get from there to <environment: namespace:stats>, which is where we're getting df from ...

Q: PostgreSQL 9.3: How to insert upper case UUID into table A:

tl;dr

UUIDs are 128-bit values, not text. The hex text you see is for human consumption, not computers.

In years past, the hexadecimal representation of a UUID was required to be all-lowercase. But no longer. You may see the hex text of a UUID in all-lowercase, all-UPPERCASE, or in mIxEDcaSe.

👉🏽 If you want a particular case (lower or upper), from any system (Postgres or otherwise), be sure to convert the hex text yourself. Never assume.

UUID is not text

You have misunderstood the essence of a UUID. A UUID is not text. A UUID is not composed of characters.

128 bits

A UUID is composed of 128 bits. Nothing more, nothing less.

Some of those bits have certain meaning. The meaning varies by which Version of UUID.

Hexadecimal representation

Humans do not do well when reading or writing one hundred and twenty eight 1 and 0 characters.

So when communicating with humans, we use a canonical representation where the 12 bits are converted into 32 hexadecimal representation. The hex digits (0-9, a-f/A-F) are grouped with hyphen characters as a delimiter, for a total of 36 characters.

For example:

019dcb4d-bd9f-7180-96ac-b54e8ad92e39

Native UUID in Postgres

Postgres has for decades supported UUID as a native data type. This means UUID values are stored as 128 bits. Postgres does not store hex characters.

When you retrieve a UUID value for display on the console, the value is converted to hexadecimal characters rather sending 128 0 & 1 characters.

UUID specification

UUIDs have been formally defined in a written specification for decades. This is a large part of the success of UUIDs across the industry.

The two most recent specs have been managed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). The earlier one, RFC 4122, was obsoleted by RFC 9562 in 2024.

The previous spec required the hexadecimal representation to be in lowercase, while also requiring implementations to parse UPPERCASE inputs.

Unfortunately, many popular implementations violated this requirement. At one point, Microsoft even released an implementation with miXEdCaSE (good grief!).

So in the current spec, RFC 9562, the authors abandoned that all-lowercase requirement. Any case is allowed for input and for output of hexadecimal representation.

Q: Can someone explain to me why we use surrogate keys for joining some fact/dim tables? A:

I'm not sure who told you that you use surrogate keys for the join you show, because in that example, you are not using surrogate keys.

You seem to be using row numbers, which are not surrogate keys. This is not a good choice for joining, because row numbers might change if you insert or delete rows in the dimension tables, or if you update the columns used for ordering the row number (e.g. cst_id, prd_start_dt, prd_key). If the row numbers change, they won't join to the correct rows in the sales details.

Typically you join by one or more values, not by row position. There are situations in which you might join based on row number, but those situations are rare.

Q: Convergence of integral using complex integration A:

The convergence at the lower limit $z \to 0$ can be understood by looking at the behavior of the integrand's periodic component. While it's true that the denominator approaches $1$, the integral doesn't diverge because it's a conditional convergence scenario, similar to the Dirichlet integral.

1. Analysis of the lower limit ($z \to 0$):

Near the origin, the expression behaves like:

$$\int_{0}^{\epsilon} \frac{e^{iz \dots}}{1 + \dots} dz \approx \int_{0}^{\epsilon} e^{iz} dz$$

The term $e^{iz} = \cos(z) + i\sin(z)$ is bounded. Since we are integrating over a finite interval near $0$, and the integrand is continuous and bounded in that neighborhood (it doesn't have a singularity at $z=0$), the integral over $[0, \epsilon]$ is finite.

2. Convergence at the upper limit ($z \to \infty$):

As you noted, the $e^{-z}$ (or similar decaying exponential terms typically found in Landau's contour deformations) ensures absolute convergence at infinity.

3. Why Contour Integration works here:

When Landau and Lifshitz use contour integration, they usually close the contour in the upper half-plane. The "oscillations" you see on the real axis become exponential decay once you move into the complex plane ($z = x + iy$):

$$e^{iz} = e^{i(x+iy)} = e^{ix} e^{-y}$$

This $e^{-y}$ term is what makes the integral beautifully convergent as we move away from the real axis. The integral along the real axis is then defined as the limit of the contour, often handled via the Jordan's Lemma.

Summary: The integral is perfectly well-defined. The oscillations at the lower limit don't cause divergence because the integrand stays bounded as $z \to 0$, and the interval of "weak" decay is finite.

Q: YouTube IFrame API: Is conditional autoplay queue progression required when document.visibilityState is 'hidden'? A:

Don't worry. Option A and Option B are both ok and within compliance of Youtube policies.

Youtube simply does not want a scenario where: People can hear sound of YT video but cannot stop it (because the YT player is hidden to user), or worse is that a player with something like .visibility.hidden is playing a muted video (trying to get a higher YT views count based on the page visitor numbers).

A player should always be visible somewhere on your page for control by user. Minimization is a user choice and cannot be your problem.

Q: Mixing GCC/LLVM C2y preprocessor vector extension with arrays and alternatives for LLVM __builtin_vectorelements in GCC A:

Short answer: there’s no direct GCC equivalent to __builtin_vectorelements.

Use sizeof(vec) / sizeof(vec[0]) for element count, or wrap it in a macro. For generic handling, combine _Generic + sizeof or rely on GCC vector extensions (__attribute__((vector_size))) and compute length manually.

Q: How to handle ￼ (object replacement character) in URL A:

I found the issue resolved by just replacing URLs with this symbol because there are other URLs with Unicode symbols that were invisible that couldnt be converted ect..

So I just compared the urls to the following regex if it returns false then I just bypass it. Hope this helps someone out:

boolean newURL = url.matches("^[a-zA-Z0-9_:;/.&|%!+=@?-]*$");
